doc.title: Anne Phillips interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, February 24, 2025

title: Introduction; surviving the music business, clubs and Associated demos
summary: Phillips says she survived by playing piano and singing, working clubs opposite Bobby Short and then demos at Associated alongside young songwriters.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: My name is Monk Rowe for the Fillius Jazz Archive. I’m very pleased to have Anne Phillips with me today. And I won’t do a complete introduction because that would take too long. So I’ll say vocalist, composer, producer, and a general survivor of the music business.
What makes the music business something that you describe as being a survivor of?

Well let’s see — I know too many people who haven’t survived. I was very fortunate because I played piano. I could play piano and sing. And so when I came to New York I didn’t have to wait tables. I’ve done nothing in my life but music. And then the music business began, which is first playing in clubs, some lovely ones. Like I played actually opposite Bobby Short in his first gig at the — it wasn’t the Carlyle then it was the Beverly Hotel, and I was the other, the off piano. And I sat there writing names of songs and lyrics down, things I’d never heard. And then I found out about demos for songwriters, and it was a wonderful time. There were the older songwriters and there were the new kids coming in like Carole King and Gerry Goffin and Ellie Greenwich and Neil Sedaka, all those people. And there was a little studio that did most of them, Associated, and some of us who have survived the whole thing say we ought to call it “Associated University” because we learned everything there.
